questions.question: What is SDLC and why is it important?
questions.answer: SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is a structured process with six phases — Requirement Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Maintenance — that guides how software is built. It is important because it ensures software is built systematically, with quality checks at each stage, reducing costly mistakes and rework. Without SDLC, teams would write code randomly without understanding requirements, leading to software that doesn't meet user needs.

questions.question: What are the six phases of SDLC in order?
questions.answer: 1. Requirement Analysis — understand business needs. 2. Design — plan architecture, database, UI. 3. Development — write the code. 4. Testing — check for bugs, performance, security. 5. Deployment — make the app live. 6. Maintenance — release updates, fix issues.

questions.question: What is the difference between Waterfall and Agile?
questions.answer: Waterfall is sequential and rigid — each phase must be completed fully before the next begins. It works well when requirements are fixed and well-defined. Agile is iterative and flexible — software is delivered in short sprint cycles with continuous feedback. Agile is better for dynamic projects where requirements evolve. Most modern companies use Agile.

questions.question: What is the difference between a program, software, and an application?
questions.answer: A program is a set of instructions written in a programming language. Software is one or more programs packaged together to solve a problem — it runs on a computer and is not the end user. An application is software specifically designed for an end user to perform a task. Example: a Python script is a program; Microsoft Office is software; Gmail is an application.

questions.question: Explain the client-server model.
questions.answer: In the client-server model, a client (browser, mobile app, or device) sends a request to a server. The server (a powerful computer or software) processes the request and sends back a response. This is the foundation of every web application — the client requests, the server responds. For example, when you open amazon.com, your browser (client) sends a request, and Amazon's servers respond with the web page.

questions.question: What is an IP address? What is a port?
questions.answer: An IP address is a unique numerical identifier for every device on a network — like a street address that tells data where to go. A port is a numbered 'door' on a server that identifies which specific service should receive the request — like an apartment number in a building. The IP gets data to the right server; the port directs it to the right service on that server. Common ports: HTTP=80, HTTPS=443, SSH=22, MySQL=3306.

questions.question: What is CapEx vs OpEx in the context of IT infrastructure?
questions.answer: CapEx (Capital Expenditure) is the upfront cost of purchasing physical assets — servers, storage, networking gear, data center space. You pay a lot once and own the hardware. OpEx (Operational Expenditure) is recurring costs for ongoing operations — electricity, salaries, cloud subscriptions. Cloud computing converts CapEx to OpEx: instead of buying servers (CapEx), you rent them by the hour (OpEx), paying only for what you use.

questions.question: What is cloud computing? Name three major cloud providers.
questions.answer: Cloud computing is the delivery of IT resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, software — over the internet on a pay-as-you-go basis. Instead of owning infrastructure, you rent it from a cloud provider and use it on demand. Three major providers: Amazon Web Services (AWS) — market leader with 200+ services; Microsoft Azure — strong enterprise integration; Google Cloud Platform (GCP) — leading in AI/ML and Kubernetes.

questions.question: Why do businesses prefer cloud over on-premise infrastructure?
questions.answer: Businesses prefer cloud because: (1) No upfront CapEx — pay only for what you use; (2) Instant provisioning — spin up servers in minutes, not weeks; (3) Elastic scaling — automatically handle traffic spikes; (4) Global reach — deploy in any region instantly; (5) High availability — built-in redundancy; (6) Managed security — provider handles physical security. The business can focus on its product instead of managing IT infrastructure.

questions.question: What are the different types of servers? Give examples of each.
questions.answer: Web Server: handles HTTP/HTTPS requests and serves web pages. Examples: Apache, Nginx. Application Server: runs business logic and API processing. Examples: Node.js, Tomcat, Django. Database Server: stores and retrieves data. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL (SQL), MongoDB (NoSQL). File Server: stores and shares files. Examples: Samba, FTP, AWS S3. In a modern app, all four types work together in a layered architecture.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder. How did you approach it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A business owner needed to understand why we recommended migrating to cloud versus keeping on-premise servers — he was skeptical about the cost. (Task) I needed to explain the financial and operational benefits without using jargon. (Action) I used the 'rent vs buy' analogy: instead of buying a car (CapEx — expensive, depreciates, you maintain it), you use a cab service like Uber (OpEx — pay per ride, no maintenance). I then showed a side-by-side cost comparison demonstrating 40% savings by eliminating idle server capacity. (Result) He approved the cloud migration within the week.

questions.question: Describe a situation where your team skipped or rushed a SDLC phase. What happened?
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team was under pressure to deliver a feature before a product launch, so the testing phase was compressed from 2 weeks to 2 days. (Task) We needed to ship a payment integration. (Action) We pushed to production with minimal testing. (Result) A critical bug caused duplicate charges for some customers. We had to roll back, issue refunds, and delay the launch anyway — costing 3x the time we thought we'd saved. Lesson: rushing Testing phase always costs more in the long run.

questions.question: You're asked to architect a simple web application for a small business. Describe the basic infrastructure components you'd set up on AWS.
questions.answer: (Situation) A small business needs a product catalog website. (Task) Set up cloud infrastructure. (Action) I'd set up: an EC2 instance (virtual server) for the web and application server, an RDS instance (database server) for MySQL, an S3 bucket for static files and images, a security group (virtual firewall) allowing HTTP/HTTPS on ports 80/443, and a domain via Route 53. (Result) A fully functional, secure, cost-effective application using cloud's pay-as-you-go model — no hardware to buy or maintain.

questions.question: A client complains their website is slow during morning hours and fast the rest of the day. What's likely happening and how would cloud help?
questions.answer: (Situation) Traffic spikes every morning when users log in at the start of their workday. (Task) Diagnose and fix. (Action) The slowdown is a capacity issue — the server is overwhelmed during peak hours. With on-premise, you'd need to overprovision for peak, wasting money all day. With cloud, I'd implement auto-scaling: automatically add servers when load increases and remove them when it decreases. (Result) The site handles peak traffic seamlessly, and costs remain low during off-peak hours because extra servers are terminated.

questions.question: Your team is building a product for a government agency. Requirements are fully documented and locked. Should you use Agile or Waterfall? Defend your choice.
questions.answer: (Situation) Government contract with locked, fully documented requirements and mandatory phase-completion sign-offs for compliance. (Task) Choose SDLC methodology. (Action) Waterfall is the right choice here. Reasons: Requirements are stable — Agile's iteration adds no value when there's nothing to iterate on. Government compliance often requires formal documentation and sign-off at each phase boundary. Audit trails are cleaner in Waterfall. (Result) Delivered on-time with full regulatory documentation. Note: I would still advocate for automated testing within each phase to mitigate Waterfall's testing risks.

questions.question: Explain how an e-commerce purchase flows through a 3-tier architecture.
questions.answer: (Situation) User clicks 'Buy Now' on an e-commerce site. Full 3-tier flow: (1) Browser (client) sends HTTPS POST request to the Web Server (Nginx/Apache) on port 443. (2) Web Server forwards the request to the Application Server (Node.js/Python) which validates the purchase, checks inventory, processes payment via payment gateway API, and applies discount logic. (3) Application Server queries the Database Server (MySQL) to deduct inventory, create an order record, and log the transaction. (4) Database sends results back up the chain. (5) Application Server sends confirmation. (6) Web Server sends the 'Order Confirmed' response to the browser. Total round-trip: typically under 500ms.

questions.question: A startup is choosing between on-premise servers and AWS. Walk me through the key considerations.
questions.answer: (Situation) Startup with unpredictable growth trajectory. (Task) Evaluate on-premise vs cloud. (Action) Key considerations: Budget — on-premise requires heavy CapEx upfront; AWS is OpEx with no upfront. Scalability — on-premise scaling takes weeks; AWS scales in minutes. Expertise — on-premise requires dedicated sysadmin team; AWS can be managed by developers. Risk — on-premise: you own failures; AWS: SLA guarantees 99.99% uptime. For a startup, AWS wins: low upfront cost, scales with growth, DevOps team can focus on product. Exception: high data sovereignty requirements or extremely predictable stable workloads might favor on-premise.

questions.question: How does the pay-as-you-go model benefit a company with seasonal traffic peaks?
questions.answer: (Situation) An e-commerce company has 10x traffic during Diwali sale versus normal days. (Task) Optimize infrastructure cost. (Action) With pay-as-you-go cloud: scale up 10x during the Diwali week (10 servers), then scale back to 1 server the rest of the year. Pay only for those 10 servers during the sale period. Compare to on-premise: buy 10 servers for the peak, have 9 sitting idle 95% of the year — paying depreciation, power, and maintenance for all 10 year-round. (Result) Cloud typically delivers 60-80% cost savings for seasonal workloads.

questions.question: A new developer joins your team and asks: 'What's the difference between a web server and an application server?' How do you explain it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Onboarding a junior developer. (Task) Explain web vs application server clearly. (Action) Analogy: imagine a restaurant. The web server is the front desk — it greets customers (browsers), takes their order (HTTP request), and delivers the plate (HTML response). The application server is the kitchen — it does the actual cooking (business logic, calculations, auth checks, API calls). The web server handles the 'presentation layer'; the app server handles the 'logic layer'. In a real app, Nginx (web server) receives requests and forwards complex ones to Node.js (app server) which talks to MySQL (database server). (Result) Developer understood immediately and correctly configured routing the next day.

questions.question: Your cloud bill was 3x higher than expected this month. What are your first three diagnostic steps?
questions.answer: (Situation) Unexpected cloud bill spike. (Task) Diagnose root cause. (Action) Step 1: Check AWS Cost Explorer — identify which service had the highest spend increase (EC2, S3, data transfer, etc.). Step 2: Look for resources that weren't terminated — development servers left running 24/7, large snapshots, orphaned volumes. Step 3: Check data transfer costs — often overlooked. Transferring data OUT of AWS incurs charges; unexpected spikes could mean a misconfigured app making redundant API calls or a DDoS attack generating traffic. Longer term: set up billing alerts so you're notified before the bill surprises you.

questions.question: Compare AWS, Azure, and GCP — when would you recommend each?
questions.answer: AWS: Recommend when the team needs the broadest service catalog, highest market adoption, or the most available talent/certifications. Best for startups, diverse workloads, and teams building for scale from day one. Azure: Recommend for enterprises already deeply invested in Microsoft technologies — Office 365, Active Directory, Windows Server. Azure's hybrid cloud integrations make it the natural choice for enterprises with on-premise Microsoft infrastructure. GCP: Recommend for teams heavily invested in AI/ML (Vertex AI, TensorFlow), containerized workloads (GKE — Google invented Kubernetes), or large-scale analytics (BigQuery). Also a strong choice if you're already using Google Workspace.

questions.question: Explain the concept of 'infrastructure as code' and how it relates to SDLC.
questions.answer: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means managing cloud infrastructure — servers, networks, databases — through code files (e.g., AWS CloudFormation, Terraform) rather than manual console clicks. Relationship to SDLC: Design phase defines the infrastructure architecture. Development phase includes writing IaC scripts alongside application code. Testing phase tests both the app AND the infrastructure (does the CloudFormation template deploy correctly?). Deployment phase uses the IaC to provision production infrastructure consistently. Maintenance phase updates IaC when infrastructure changes. IaC brings software engineering practices (version control, code review, automated testing) to infrastructure management — the key to modern DevOps.

questions.question: A company operates in a regulated industry (healthcare, banking) and wants to move to cloud. What architectural concerns must you address?
questions.answer: Key concerns: (1) Data Residency — regulations may require data to stay in specific countries. Verify that the cloud provider has data centers in those regions (AWS regions in India: Mumbai, Hyderabad). (2) Encryption — all data at rest and in transit must be encrypted. Cloud provides tools, but you must configure and manage encryption keys. (3) Access Control — implement strict IAM policies: least privilege, MFA, audit logging. (4) Compliance Certifications — AWS holds certifications for HIPAA (healthcare), PCI-DSS (payments), SOC 2, ISO 27001. Verify your architecture meets these. (5) Audit Trails — enable AWS CloudTrail for all API activity logging. (6) Shared Responsibility — understand what the provider covers vs what you must manage.

questions.question: How would you design a highly available, cost-optimized application for an e-commerce startup on AWS?
questions.answer: High Availability: Deploy across at least 2 Availability Zones (AZs) to survive data center failures. Use a Load Balancer to distribute traffic between multiple EC2 instances. Use RDS Multi-AZ for database failover. Store static assets in S3 (99.999999999% durability). Cost Optimization: Use Auto Scaling to match capacity to demand — scale up on traffic spikes, down during quiet hours. Use Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for baseline load (up to 72% discount vs On-Demand). Use spot instances for non-critical batch jobs. Use CloudFront CDN to cache content near users, reducing origin server load. Set billing alerts in AWS Budgets. Result: The architecture handles traffic spikes automatically, recovers from failures without downtime, and only pays for what it actually uses.

questions.question: Explain the 'shared responsibility model' in cloud computing. How does it change security responsibilities?
questions.answer: The Shared Responsibility Model defines who is responsible for what in cloud security. AWS is responsible FOR the cloud: physical data center security, network infrastructure, hypervisor, storage hardware, and global networking. The Customer is responsible IN the cloud: operating system patching, application security, data encryption, access management (IAM), network configuration (Security Groups, VPCs), and compliance with regulations. Practical implication: If AWS's physical data center is breached, that's AWS's problem. If your EC2 instance is hacked because you left port 22 open to the internet with a weak password, that's your problem. This model means cloud security requires you to actively configure and manage your portion — it doesn't make security automatic.
